extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars seeking an encyclopedia-style overview of Mark Twain's life, works, and views
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic biographical article summarizing Mark Twain's life, major works, stylistic views, political positions, controversies, and legacy. Intended as a comprehensive reference overview rather than a focused how-to or critical essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality writing (Twain's criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain outlines what he considers to be "quality writing" in several letters and essays, placing emphasis on concision, utility of word choice, and realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: focus on concision, choose words for utility, and aim for realism. Twain used these standards when criticizing other authors (example: his criticisms of Cooper's Deerslayer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and organization in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics have cited lack of continuity (Adventures of Huckleberry Finn) and rough organization or constant disruption of the plot (Pudd'nhead Wilson) as faults tied to rushed completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit guidance: avoid rushed writing; ensure structural cohesion, continuity, and clear plot organization. The page links rushed composition (e.g., writing 60,000 words in a month) to declines in organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative ending and authorial 'failure of nerve' (evaluative end-of-work judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The last fifth of Huckleberry Finn is 'subject to much controversy' with some critics (e.g., Leo Marx) and Ernest Hemingway arguing the book should effectively end earlier, calling the remainder 'just cheating.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating a work: whether its ending preserves the integrity and tone of the earlier parts; endings that diverge sharply from established tone or moral arc may be judged as weakenings or failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation/attribution affects reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain specifically insisted Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc be published anonymously so that readers would take it as a serious historical account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: how a work is attributed or presented (anonymous vs. by a known author) can change readers' reception and perceived seriousness; authors may choose presentation strategies to influence credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial suitability for target publication/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Prayer was rejected by Harper's Bazaar as 'not quite suited to a woman's magazine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for submitting/publishing: align content and tone with the target publication's audience and editorial expectations; provocative or controversial pieces may be refused if perceived as mismatched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language suitability for children and censorship risk
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1905 the Brooklyn Public Library banned both The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer from the children's department because of their language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: use of language (esp. profanity or racial epithets) affects suitability for young readers and can provoke censorship or removal from children's collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire as a device to reveal social/political absurdities
rubrics_metrics.description: Works like A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court and King Leopold's Soliloquy use satire to show the absurdities of political and social norms; Twain's essays (e.g., To the Person Sitting in Darkness) employ sardonic suggestions and political pamphleteering to critique imperialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/examples: use irony, sardonic proposals, exaggeration and inversion to expose hypocrisy and criticize power; satire can reach beyond humor to serious political argument (examples: attacks on imperialism, missionary indemnities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of authorial structure to retain humor and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain dictated his autobiography with whims and tangents in non-chronological order because he thought it would be most entertaining; archivists who rearranged it removed some of Twain's humor and flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for editors/compilers: altering an author's original structure (chronology, tangents, digressions) can diminish intended humor and the work's entertainments; preservation of original form may be crucial to authorial effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal experience and authenticity in voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain's riverboat experience and related anecdotes (including the origin story of the pen name 'Mark Twain') are presented as contributing to an authentic, authoritative voice—'a sign and symbol and warrant that whatever is found in its company may be gambled on as being the petrified truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: grounding humor and narrative in personal experience or documented detail can lend credibility and distinctive voice to writing; anecdotal authenticity enhances reader trust and comedic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/humanitarian conscience as a component of authorial persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain's later writing shows strong anti-imperialist and humanitarian stances (e.g., The War Prayer, The Incident in the Philippines), using moral outrage as part of his public voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: authors may combine humor/satire with explicit moral or political critique; the seriousness of the underlying convictions can shape tone and reception—satire is not purely for entertainment but can be deployed as moral argument.
